News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:18:05 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>Europe</category><title>Why Ukraine keeps trying to bring down Russia's bridge to Crimea</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261118-why-ukraine-keeps-trying-to-bring-down-russia-s-bridge-to-crimea</link><description>
A Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Monday night brought down a stretch of the bridge linking the annexed Crimean Peninsula to Russia, potentially crippling a route long used by Moscow to move men and materiel into Crimea and the southern front. Here’s why Kyiv keeps testing its strength against an infrastructure project that has become synonymous with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 2014 seizure of the peninsula.  
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/6b1cf78a-e374-11f1-ae39-1ba7ddfab527/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-17T132708Z-373589621-RC2PPOA5FXQR-RTRMADP-3-UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-CRIMEA-SBU.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/6b1cf78a-e374-11f1-ae39-1ba7ddfab527/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-17T132708Z-373589621-RC2PPOA5FXQR-RTRMADP-3-UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-CRIMEA-SBU.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">f055bd98-e373-11f1-a1da-21f28020077c</guid><pubDate>Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:17:34 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/6b1cf78a-e374-11f1-ae39-1ba7ddfab527/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-17T132708Z-373589621-RC2PPOA5FXQR-RTRMADP-3-UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-CRIMEA-SBU.jpg">© Security Service of Ukraine handout via Reuters</source><dc:creator>Paul MILLAR</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Beijing has supported Moscow but 'China understands that America is way more important than Russia'</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/beijing-has-supported-moscow-but-china-understands-that-america-is-way-more-important-than-russia</link><description>
Following Xi Jinping's very friendly rare tarmac greeting for Donald Trump, Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Kerry Brown, Professor of Chinese Studies and Director of the Lau China Institute at King's College, London. Brown examines the complex relationship between the world's two largest economies, China's growing diplomatic influence and the competition over artificial intelligence.“China is the diplomatic center of the world,” says Brown, pointing to Beijing's ability to bring together leaders from Russia, the United States, Europe and elsewhere. He argues that China now has “extraordinary convening power" and significant influence over Russia. 
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/2bed0054-e370-11f1-905e-7908c4e1a3c7/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261118-150609-151600-CS-01.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/2bed0054-e370-11f1-905e-7908c4e1a3c7/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261118-150609-151600-CS-01.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">316d86b6-e370-11f1-ad2c-13c5d8f75fe6</guid><pubDate>Wed, 18 Nov 2026 17:48:38 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>France</category><title>French ex-PM Philippe pledges to slash spending, hike retirement age as Elysée bid falters</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261118-french-ex-pm-philippe-pledges-to-slash-spending-hike-retirement-age-as-elys%C3%A9e-bid-falters</link><description>
Former prime minister Édouard Philippe pledged on Wednesday to slash public spending, scrap France’s statutory 35-hour workweek and raise the retirement age to 65 from the current 62.9 years as he unveiled a slew of measures aimed a staving off economic "catastrophe" for France. An early frontrunner in next year's presidential election, Philippe is now trailing rivals in opinion polls and at risk of missing out on the second-round runoff.

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Wed, 18 Nov 2026 20:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why ]]> More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.

Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.

Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.

One of the most striking examples is found in the Grand Canyon, where rocks separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, as if some force or phenomenon removed the layers that geologists would expect to see in between. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity.

It's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana said in a statement.

"The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance."

What erased the geological record?

In a new study published in the journal Nature, Dhungana and study co-author Nicolas Flament investigated whether activity far below Earth's surface was to blame.

Using computer models, they explored how the slow circulation of hot rock within Earth's mantle may have affected the continents over hundreds of millions of years.

The results suggest that three major ancient continental regions (Laurentia (modern North America), Baltica (northern Europe) and North China were gradually pushed up during the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately one billion to 540 million years ago.

This would have left vast areas of land exposed to weathering and erosion for long periods, allowing water, wind and other processes to wear away rock that had formed much earlier.

But removing the rock is only part of the puzzle. They also needed to explain why the gaps are still visible today.

Their models suggest that the same regions subsequently began to sink. As sea levels rose relative to the land, sediment accumulated over the older, eroded surfaces, creating the sharp divide between ancient and younger rocks that we can still see today.

Crucially, the researchers found that the timing of the simulated continental uplift and sinking was consistent with geological evidence from North America, northern Europe and North China. This suggests that movements deep within Earth's mantle may have played a major role in shaping the geological record we see today.

]]> <![CDATA[ ULA traces Vulcan Centaur rocket failure to 'inadequate fuel supply' to 1st-stage engines ]]> United Launch Alliance (ULA) is getting a handle on why its Vulcan Centaur rocket failed over the weekend.

That failure, which occurred during a launch from Florida's Space Coast on Sunday (Nov. 15), led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites. ULA soon traced the anomaly to Vulcan Centaur's first stage, and it has now pinpointed the problem area even further.

"While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines," ULA wrote in an update today (Nov. 18).

This is good news for Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos' aerospace company, which builds the BE-4. Two of these engines power Vulcan's first-stage booster, and they're also key to Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket: That heavy lifter features seven or nine BE-4s in its first stage, depending on the configuration. (New Glenn has its own issues at the moment; it exploded during a test on May 28, and Blue Origin is working to return the powerful rocket to flight.)

ULA had already said that Vulcan's six solid rocket boosters (SRBs) and its Centaur V upper stage — which employs a different engine, the RL-10 — seem to perform well on Sunday. Further analysis is firming up that conclusion, according to today's update.

Vulcan has had issues with its SRBs in the past. On the rocket's second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds into flight. On both occasions, Vulcan overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payload to orbit.

In the wake of the February flight, ULA and Northrop Grumman, which builds the SRBs, tweaked the nozzle design — a fix that apparently worked, based on Sunday's nominal performance.

Sunday's launch was the fifth ever for the two-stage Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has now experienced issues on three of its five flights, though Sunday's was the only one that ended in failure.

Vulcan was out of action for about nine months after the February SRB issue. It's unclear how long its current grounding will last; that depends on what ULA's anomaly investigation, which the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing, ends up finding.

]]> <![CDATA[ 'A shotgun marriage': Why are NASA's SkyFall Mars helicopters riding on a nuclear rocket? ]]> The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket.

NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet.

But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the "Mars Czar") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'"

Shotgun marriage?

Hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform.

Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management issues." Since the SkyFall mission concept first appeared, he said, the usual sequence for a science mission is reversed.

"The science community is having to scramble to back into a set of requirements and objectives that match the SkyFall capabilities. Fortunately the community is very creative," said Hubbard, "and the basic Planetary Decadal objectives are very broad."

Decadal surveys reflect a broad consensus within the scientific community and provide detailed insights into the strategic priorities and mission directives set for the next decade across key scientific domains, including planetary exploration.

Lemonade squeeze

However, Hubbard said he has heard griping about the "fait accompli" process, "but the planetary community will make lemonade."

It should be noted however, Hubbard continued, that this process is not how you would design a strategic set of missions as precursors for human exploration.

"SR-1 Freedom is a technology demo that may or may not be ready for the Mars launch window in 2028. It is clear that the Mars Program has a standard launch concept in their back pocket," said Hubbard. "Nuclear Electric Propulsion [NEP] is of little value in traveling to Mars, not shaving any time off the transit. The real value of NEP is for risk reduction, use at the moon, outer planets and even bolder ideas like interstellar travel," Hubbard concluded.

Resolution gap

"This, by far, is the shortest Mars mission ever conceived of," said Matthew Golombek, SkyFall Project Scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., speaking Nov. 10 during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

Kick-started by NASA in March 2026, the SkyFall project has grown from roughly six people to over 200 individuals who are now working on the initiative, said Golombek. "This is an incredibly rapid development and build," he said.

"It's really to demonstrate that exploration is possible with helicopters … filling what I call a 'resolution gap' between orbital information and surface information," Golombek told the MEPAG.

Once deployed by a helicopter deployment system, the threesome will spin up their rotors at about a kilometer above the surface of Mars. Then each helicopter lands on its own, ready to undertake flights every other solar day on the Red Planet. A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth.

What is it?

Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf.

During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion.

Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter.

This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place.

Why is it incredible?

Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres.

ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system.

But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova.

Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

]]> <![CDATA[ India's SatLeo Labs wants to build a 'thermometer for Earth' in space ]]> AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time.

SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a "thermometer for Earth" in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence, the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says.

"It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview.

That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs.

The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches.

Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai.

"We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO.

The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

Need for speed

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system."

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

NOVÉ ZASTUPITELSTVO JIŘÍKOVA ZAHÁJILO SVÉ VOLEBNÍ OBDOBÍ
(Jiříkovské noviny listopad 2026)
V pondělí 9. 11. 2026 se uskutečnilo ustavující zasedání Zastupitelstva města Jiříkov, které zahájilo nové čtyřleté volební období 2026–2030. Na programu bylo především složení slibu nově zvolených zastupitelů, volba vedení města a dalších orgánů samosprávy.
Po složení zákonem předepsaného slibu přistoupili zastupitelé k volbě starosty a místostarosty města. Starostou Jiříkova byl zvolen a svou funkci tak obhájil Ing. Bc. Jindřich Jurajda, DiS. Nikol Kopecká (Spolek přátel Jiříkova a Filipova). Součástí jednání byla také volba předsedů a členů finančního a kontrolního výboru. V čele finančního výboru usedla stejně jako v minulém volebním období Naděžda Stožická (NEZÁVISLÍ KANDIDÁTI MĚSTA JIŘÍKOVA) a předsedou kontrolního výboru se stal Mgr. Petr Kulhánek MBA (ANO 2011).
Nově zvolené vedení města tak přebírá odpovědnost za další rozvoj Jiříkova, hospodaření s městským majetkem, přípravu a realizaci investičních projektů i každodenní chod městské samosprávy.
Nové zastupitelstvo tvoří celkem 15 členů zvolených za čtyři kandidující uskupení. Jejich společným úkolem bude rozhodovat o důležitých otázkách života města a zastupovat zájmy jeho obyvatel.
Všem nově zvoleným zastupitelům přejeme hodně sil, trpělivosti a úspěchů při práci pro Jiříkov a jeho občany.
